evidence: Cic. Sen. 26: litterās Graecās senex didicī
Plaut. Aul. 595: puerī quī nāre discunt
terms.comment: With an accusative (litterās discere), an infinitive for a skill (nāre discere, learn to swim), and ab or ex aliquō for the teacher. No supine in classical Latin. To learn by heart is ēdiscere (see learn by heart).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.69: hic locus dē vītā et mōribus tōtus est ōrātōrī perdiscendus

phrases.latin: Cicerōnēs puerī amant inter sē, exercentur, sed discunt, alter … frēnīs eget, alter calcāribus
phrases.english: The boys love each other and play games, but they learn: one needs the reins, the other the spurs.

phrases.latin: aestāte puerī sī valent, satis discunt
phrases.english: In summer, if children keep well, they learn enough.

phrases.latin: alius ait hoc mē prīmum docē, item alius hoc volō, inquit, discere, istud nōlō
phrases.english: One says, “Teach me this first”; another, “I want to learn this,” he says, “not that.”

phrases.latin: hoc ante omnia fac, mī Lūcīlī: disce gaudēre
phrases.english: Above all, my Lucilius, do this: learn to be glad.
